items.blurb: Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues remain an essential resource for molecular studies, yet formalin-induced cytosine deamination introduces characteristic C>T/G>A artifacts that compromise the accuracy of next-generation sequencing (NGS) analyses. Numerous computational methods and enzymatic DNA repair strategies have been proposed to reduce these artifacts, but no systematic comparison across tools and experimental conditions exists. Here, we evaluate the performance of seven computational approaches (SOBDetector, Ideafix, MicroSEC, FFPolish, DeepOmics FFPE/FFPE-PLUS, FFPErase) together with the NEBNext FFPE DNA Repair Mix v2, a multi-enzyme repair system applied during DNA preparation. Using three independent datasets, one based on whole genome sequencing (CGCI-BL) and two on whole exome sequencing (TCGA-PC and SUT-LUAD, the latter containing enzymatically repaired samples), and matched fresh-frozen samples as the gold standard, we assess precision, sensitivity, and artifact reduction efficiency across all methods. We further examine the potential synergy between enzymatic repair and post-sequencing computational filtering. Our results provide practical guidelines for FFPE artifact correction and demonstrate that enzymatic treatment provides the best results, while among the computational methods, FFPErase offers the most robust reduction of cytosine deamination artifacts while maximizing the retention of true somatic variants.

items.title: Assessing Codon Language Models for Context-Aware Codon Optimization in Nucleic Acid-Based Medicines
items.blurb: Codon optimization uses synonymous sequence changes to improve the expression and therapeutic performance of nucleic acid-based medicines. Masked language models (MLMs) have recently been proposed as alternatives to traditional, frequency-based codon optimization approaches, yet whether they offer a meaningful advantage over such simpler methods remains unclear. Here we benchmark three prominent MLMs --- CaLM, EnCodon and CodonTransformer --- across backtranslation fidelity, sequence generation and nine molecular phenotype prediction tasks, and experimentally evaluate model-designed sequences using a secreted embryonic alkaline phosphatase (SEAP) reporter. The models differed markedly in amino-acid fidelity and generated distinct synonymous sequence variants. However, no single model performed best across all benchmark tasks and simple sequence features remained competitive in several settings. Our interpretability analysis revealed that the models integrate a large window of codon context for making predictions, as opposed to frequency-based approaches. Our in vitro data showed that MLM-designed variants outperformed conventional and commercial vendor-derived sequences in both transient and stably integrated expression, supporting the models' ability to capture translational context beyond codon frequency. Together, our results establish MLMs as effective and complementary tools for codon optimization and suggest that sampling across multiple models may improve the likelihood of identifying high-performing therapeutic sequences.

items.title: The Marginal Value Theorem in Caenorhabditis elegans
items.blurb: The Marginal Value Theorem (MVT) is an important part of Optimal Foraging Theory, predicting the optimal time to leave a food patch. It has been mostly studied in birds, insects and mammals, even though simpler organisms also need to forage efficiently in patchy environments. Here we test whether the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans implements the MVT. We recorded individual nematodes exploring patchy environments, across four inter-patch distances and three different food qualities, and found that C. elegans behavior matches MVT predictions: When food patches are further away, each food patch is exploited for a longer time. In previous studies animals achieved this by modulating the duration of visits to food patches. Similarly, we found that C. elegans also increases visit duration with inter-patch distance, but this only accounts for half of the increase in total exploitation time. The other half of the increase comes from C. elegans revisiting food patches multiple times, and the number of these revisits increasing with inter-patch distance. This increase in the number of revisits is not due to behavioral changes in response to distance, but rather to a passive interaction between trajectories and environment geometry. These results show that C. elegans can learn the statistics of an environment and use this information in a way consistent with the MVT, but also that part of the fitness-relevant outcomes can emerge passively.

items.title: Requirement of hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha for interleukin 1 beta induced glycolysis in colorectal cancer cells.
items.blurb: Colorectal cancer cells increase glycolysis to help meet the metabolic demands required for cell growth. Many factors, both endogenous and exogenous, likely drive cellular metabolism and enhance glycolytic flux in colorectal cells. Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1{beta}) is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that is elevated in colorectal cancer. In this study, we investigated the effect of IL-1{beta} toward driving the cancer cell to increase glycolysis, while also suppressing the oxidation of the fiber-derived nutrient butyrate. The results presented here demonstrate that IL-1{beta} stimulated glycolysis and inhibited maximal mitochondrial respiration. IL-1{beta} also increased the phosphorylation of AKT and hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF1) levels. Utilizing colorectal cancer cells with AKT1/2 or HIF1 knocked out showed the requirement of these proteins in mediating the increase in glycolysis following IL-1{beta} treatment. Importantly, AKT1/2 was identified as upstream of HIF1, as IL-1{beta} still increased phosphorylation of AKT even in the absence of HIF1. However, loss of AKT1/2 completely abolished the ability of IL-1{beta} to increase HIF1 protein levels. Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF), another cytokine found to be elevated in colorectal cancer, also increased glycolysis in an AKT and HIF1-dependent manner. Our data point to a common pathway through AKT activation and HIF1 upregulation, by which pro-inflammatory cytokines increase glycolysis in colorectal cancer cells to help promote cancer progression.

Here are three immutable facts about Brandon Richard Flowers: he was born just outside Las Vegas, Nevada. He is 45 years old. And he never does anything by halves. When he and his band the Killers debuted in the early 2000s, as disaffected New York cool was on the rise, he was writing scream-along choruses sung in his upper register. When the Killers were searching for a sound even bigger and grander than the euphoric Springsteen pastiche of 2006’s Sam’s Town, they didn’t think twice before recruiting Stuart Price to produce the spangly 2008 disco-rock record Day & Age.

That’s how you get a record like Thrasher. Flowers’ third solo album finds Vegas’s chosen son decamping to Nashville for a full-throated exploration of country music – not subtle, trendy Americana, but rip-snorting, honky-tonking, Nudie suit-wearing country. In many ways, Thrasher is a stylistic follow-up to the Killers’ maudlin 2021 Pressure Machine, which saw Flowers explore windswept balladry and tasteful story-songs. But that record was as forgettable as Thrasher is a hoot; Flowers wilts when he doesn’t fully commit, as was the case on Pressure Machine, and he doesn’t make that mistake here. Thrasher features many of Nashville’s most revered country musicians, including pedal steel legend Bruce Bouton, 85-year-old harmonica player Charlie McCoy, Gillian Welch’s musical partner Dave Rawlings and lauded Americana musician Margo Price.

items.title: Agrippa by Robert Harris review – persuasive portrait of rivalry in ancient Rome
items.blurb:
This fictional memoir by Octavius’s right-hand man shows us bloodshed, betrayal and hectic jockeying for power

If you’re one of those people who thinks about the Roman empire several times a week, Robert Harris has you covered. He follows his trilogy of novels about the life of Cicero and his one-off about the unpleasantness in Pompeii with a narrative that takes us from civil war through the assassination of Julius Caesar, with all the bickering and bloodshed that follows, on to the decisive battle of Actium and Octavius’s apotheosis as Caesar Augustus. We meet Cicero, Fulvia, Lepidus, two Caesars and a burly Antony (“Imagine, if you will, a statue of Hercules with a club in one hand, a wineskin in the other”).

Here’s the clever bit: he narrates it all from the point of view of Octavius’s right-hand man, Agrippa, a much less well-remembered figure. Harris tells us he “left behind no speeches, few letters and only a couple of sentences of direct quotation”. Yet Agrippa was “effective co-ruler of the Roman world for many years” and “the greatest general of the period”. Octavius couldn’t have risen without him, but he seems to have done his best to write him out of the story afterwards, according him only two passing mentions in the Res Gestae Divi Augusti.

items.blurb:

  • Sign up for our free newsletter here

There are caveats. It was only the Community Shield – and no side has gone on to win the league after lifting the Community Shield since 2018. It was against the league champions, whose preseason has involved far less strenuous travel than their own. By the time the season really gets going, there will be greater clarity in central midfield, with Rodri set to complete his move to Barcelona imminently. But this was a startlingly bad opening for Enzo Maresca at Manchester City.

Succeeding a manager of Pep Guardiola’s stature is never easy, as numerous clubs have found. But it’s not just Guardiola’s stature, the sense that whoever follows him stands in his shadow. It’s that his style of play is so idiosyncratic that the transition process inevitably becomes more difficult. Even though Maresca was Guardiola’s assistant at City in 2022-23, and his football is Guardiola-inspired, it is not identical, not least because Guardiola was always evolving. Even allowing for all that, though, it was remarkable how poorly City defended in their 3-0 defeat to Arsenal on Sunday.

items.title: How Australia found themselves on the wrong side of cricket’s most profound upset | Geoff Lemon
items.blurb:
Despite overwhelming odds against them, Bangladesh still found a way to win – but their success wasn’t down to any Australian complacency

Sport coverage is powered by hyperbole and recency bias, but the following statement is justifiable: Bangladesh’s defeat of Australia in Darwin is the most profound upset, the greatest revolt against the pre-game odds, in international cricket history. Australia’s win in England in 1882 so shocked locals that they published a cremation-themed obituary, but the same result had already happened four times on the other side of the world. Zimbabwe stunned India in 1998, but that was at least in the underdogs’ home conditions.

India’s bench-depth win at the Gabba in 2021 has a claim, or the new nation of Pakistan winning either in India in 1952 or England in 1954. But in truth, Sunday’s result is now the title holder, not just because of the disparity between the resources and histories of the two teams, not just because of the location, but because of the manufactured rarity of this match-up even taking place. Since Bangladesh’s admission to Test ranks in 2000, Cricket Australia have treated a cricket populace of well over 100 million people with the most blatant condescension.

items.title: Born Blind, He Fought a High Court Battle for Engineering. Today, He’s a Software Vice President
items.blurb: Forty years ago, in a small hospital in Andhra Pradesh, a doctor told a young couple that their newborn son was blind. The whispers began almost immediately. What life will he ever have? He will end up begging. This is a curse on the family. But lying in that hospital bed, his mother made a promise that would shape the course of her son's entire life. "My son will not beg. He will not live in shame. Even if I must stand against the world, I will make him walk with dignity," she told her family. That son is Nagababu Jannu, and his mother’s promise would stay with him through every chapter of his life. It carried him from a small town in Andhra Pradesh to a High Court battle that changed admission rules for blind students across the state, and eventually to a Vice President’s chair at a global technology firm. A childhood shaped by hardship Nagababu was born blind in Vuyyuru, a small town in Andhra Pradesh, into a family struggling with poverty and instability. His father was a cycle mechanic who battled alcoholism, while his mother stitched cloth bags late into the night to help keep the family afloat. Growing up, Nagababu heard people define his future before he was old enough to define it for himself. Many around him believed that blindness automatically meant a life of dependence. His mother refused to accept that narrative. Long before he was fighting institutions, Nagababu was learning to question the assumptions people made about what a blind child could become. He was enrolled first at a government school for blind children in Hyderabad, where the family had relocated, before moving to the Devnar School for the Blind. It was here, he says, that he discovered the transformative power of education, technology, and teachers who believed in possibilities rather than limitations. It was also at Devnar that he met Lingam Pavan Kumar, with whom he would build one of the most enduring friendships of his life. “We met at the school for the blind where both of us studied,” Pavan Kumar recalls. The two boys, as it turned out, were also from the same village, a coincidence that "brought us closer," he says. "We have become so close that we supported each other in everything," across periods of hardship and moments of happiness. Then, in 2001, as a Class 9 student, Nagababu sat before a computer for the first time — an object that was still a novelty for most sighted Indians, let alone a blind teenager in a small-town school. "I came to know that even the blind can work on a computer," he recalls. It was a discovery that would reshape the rest of his life. A counter that said no After Class 10, Nagababu chose to pursue engineering, and decided a polytechnic diploma would be his way in. The application process, back then, was entirely offline. He and his mother travelled to buy the form in person. At the counter, they were told plainly: candidates with more than 40 percent disability were not eligible to apply. A computer screen opened up a possibility Nagababu had never been shown before: that technology could become a tool for independence, not a barrier. Nagababu did not turn back. "I wanted to go ahead and apply," he says of that moment. He did, receiving a roll number and appearing for the exam with a scribe who, he says, struggled to read the question paper properly. According to him, he was lucky to have her there at all. Despite the odds, he qualified, although his rank was not outstanding. At counselling, the same rejection awaited him. Someone even suggested he consider training as a telephone operator instead — an option put to a boy barely out of his early teens who had a very different plan for his life. "I said, I know how to get an education… I want to learn something, I want to continue my education," he remembers telling them. “We have to be treated equally, I thought." Nagababu fought this battle alone in the counselling hall, while Pavan Kumar was preparing to confront a similar barrier. Back at Devnar, he and Pavan Kumar had, while still in Class 10, discussed and agreed that Pavan Kumar too should pursue polytechnic and a diploma in engineering. Pavan Kumar would go on to face an almost identical wall — denied admission at counselling despite qualifying. He too eventually took his case to the High Court and won, after a committee was constituted to examine his eligibility for the engineering course. "The committee asked doctors to conduct a series of tests to assess his abilities," Pavan Kumar says of the ordeal, which he passed before finally being granted admission. Five minutes that changed everything Nagababu took his case straight to the Commissioner of Technical Education, invoking the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995, which was already in force. Every classroom came with its own set of obstacles, but Nagababu kept finding ways to make an education designed for sighted students work for him. "I told him that I'm not asking for a job. I want to learn something, I want to continue my education," he said. The meeting lasted barely five minutes. It was enough. The Commissioner understood his intent, Nagababu says, and granted him admission to college. But the fight for an equal education was far from over. When engineering became a legal battle Once in polytechnic college, engineering drawing became one of Nagababu’s biggest challenges. His lecturer worked with him one-on-one, using a tactile mesh board. Objects were placed on the board so Nagababu could feel their shapes and understand technical diagrams through touch . “That is how I learned all my engineering concepts,” he says. But other hurdles remained. The State Board of Technical Education did not allow him to take certain exams until he met additional requirements. His practical exams from the first year were also left unevaluated, which meant he had to take them again. When diagrams could not be seen, they had to be felt. For Nagababu, touch became another way of understanding the language of engineering. After facing repeated refusals, Nagababu approached the High Court. Since the case could take years, a presentation was arranged before several government departments in July 2005. Two months later, a university agreed to assess him directly. During a six-to-seven-hour session, examiners asked him how he wrote programs, assembled components and navigated independently. “They asked me questions back,” he recalls. In October 2005, a government order was issued allowing Nagababu to pursue engineering. The order applied beyond Nagababu’s case, opening the path for other blind students as well. Nagababu went on to complete both a Polytechnic diploma and a BTech in Computer Science, a journey he says made him the first blind person in India to achieve both qualifications. The people who kept him going None of this happened without cost. The legal battle brought expenses that were, in Nagababu's words, "out of the imagination." Nagababu’s story is not about overcoming blindness. It is about refusing to let other people’s ideas of blindness determine the size of his life. A schoolteacher stepped in to support him financially through the proceedings, and once the government order came through, the S R Gudlavalleru Engineering College agreed to sponsor his entire education and boarding, arranging evening classes to help him catch up on the semester lost to litigation. Through it all, his mother was his constant. "My mother used to take me to school every day and stayed back there, and back home in the evening," he says. His grandmother stood firmly behind him too, even as much of the extended family discouraged the path he had chosen. His father, despite his own struggles, arranged a computer for his son and covered fees before the college later waived them entirely. From his first project to a Vice President role Nagababu secured a campus placement in 2007, though the offer came only after additional telephonic rounds once the company grew unsure of hiring him. The 2008 recession delayed his joining, and he finally began work at Wipro Technologies in 2009, starting on a small project before being confirmed as a Project Engineer. "I was performing very well," he says simply. The workplace that once seemed unsure about hiring him eventually became a space where his skills, rather than his eyesight, did the talking. More than 17 years and several companies later, Nagababu today serves as Vice President and Lead Software Engineer at a global financial institution, navigating code line by line with a keyboard and screen-reading software such as JAWS and NVDA. The fight isn’t over yet Even today, barriers persist. Nagababu recalls waiting two months in 2010 to open a salary account, which was resolved only after he wrote directly to the bank's Managing Director. A similar refusal at another bank in 2013 required escalation before it was resolved. As recently as last week, he approached a bank for a loan and heard a familiar line: "We will not work with blindness." "Even in 2026, this is the case," he says, pointing to what he believes is the deeper issue: a lack of awareness, also reflected in websites and apps that leave buttons unlabelled for screen readers, despite the accessibility guidelines intended to guide them. ‘Vision & eyesight are not the same’ In 2023, Nagababu underwent major spinal fusion surgery and was left with chronic nerve pain that he still lives with. Then, while finishing his memoir, The Unseen Path , he was diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Even during treatment, he kept working on the book, reviewing proofs from the oncology ward. He chose not to stop. "Vision and eyesight are not the same thing," he says. "Vision is the ability to keep moving forward when circumstances become uncertain. It is the decision to continue building, learning, and contributing, even when life demands more from you than you thought possible." The Unseen Path traces this entire journey, from his mother's promise in a small-town hospital to a career in global technology leadership. To make it accessible to everyone, Nagababu has also released the book as a free audiobook podcast on YouTube. Nagababu’s story is not about overcoming blindness. It is about refusing to let other people’s ideas of blindness determine the size of his life. Pavan Kumar, now a manager at the State Bank of India, has seen Nagababu’s journey from close quarters. He has faced setbacks of his own too. After qualifying for a job in 2009, his joining was delayed for years. Perhaps that is why the two friends understand each other so well. Speaking about Pavan, Nagababu says his old schoolmate “never lost his spirit. There are ups and downs, but he never lost his spirit.” Pavan, in turn, remembers that financial struggles were among the things that weighed most heavily on Nagababu. “I give him confidence. He was confident, but sometimes multiple problems at a time will shut you down,” he says. Their friendship has lasted through school, careers, setbacks and years of uncertainty. For Pavan, it carries a lesson many people can relate to: sometimes, when life feels overwhelming, having someone who reminds you to keep going can make all the difference. “Being a human, we will always face problems, but we should never give up our courage,” he says. "If we believe that something can be solved, the universe will support us one way or the other. Keep your belief and keep moving forward. Always chase your dreams. You will succeed at one point in time. Believe in your hard work, not luck. Then you will succeed one day for sure."

Did you know that there is a major Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and it’s on track to be the deadliest ever? It is already the second-worst Ebola outbreak in history, with the fastest community transmission we have ever seen. It’s estimated that there have been at least 4,900 cases and more than 2,300 deaths, giving a mortality rate close to 50%. The situation is bad. That’s the consensus among global health experts.

Yet this Ebola outbreak isn’t attracting much media or public attention. If I compare it with working on the 2014 Ebola outbreak, the current silence is astounding. That year, Ebola was one of the most Googled terms in the world, covered regularly on broadcast news in many countries outside the region, attracting newspaper headlines and magazine covers. Perhaps everyone is just tired of disease after the pandemic – Covid-19 fatigue, as it’s called. Trust me, no one wants to hear about infectious diseases.

items.title: When Floodwater Hides the Roads, How Do Drones Show Rescuers Where to Go?
items.blurb: When floodwater enters a village, one of the first questions rescuers need answered is surprisingly simple: Where is the water, and who is still there? From the ground, finding that answer can be difficult. Roads may be submerged, bridges damaged and entire neighbourhoods cut off. A rescue team may know that a village is flooded, but not which roads are still passable, which homes are surrounded by water or where people are stranded. This is where a small flying machine can offer a very different view. During the recent floods in Gujarat, Mehsana-based Prime UAV deployed drones in Dholka, Ahmedabad, to support rescue teams. With some areas inaccessible to tractors and boats, the drones provided aerial surveillance, including at night, and helped teams identify areas where people needed assistance. They were also used to deliver food and water packets in waterproof payload boxes to locations that were difficult to reach by road. But how does a drone turn a flooded landscape into information that rescuers can actually use? First, it gives rescuers a view from above Think of a drone as an extra pair of eyes in the sky. Instead of sending people into potentially dangerous floodwater to inspect every road and house, a drone can fly over an affected area and capture detailed images using cameras and other sensors. During a flood, drones can do more than survey the damage — some can carry food, water and essential supplies to people cut off by rising water. Photograph: (AI generated) These images can then be processed using specialised software to create an orthomosaic map — a large, detailed aerial map made by combining hundreds of overlapping photographs. With repeated flights, teams can also track how the flood is changing: where water is spreading, which roads have disappeared underwater and which areas are becoming accessible again. So, where does the “mapping” happen? The useful part is not just the drone flying. It is what happens to the information it collects. A drone can capture overlapping photographs along a planned flight path. Mapping software identifies common points across those images and combines them into a single map. For more detailed surveys, drones can also use technologies such as LiDAR and RTK GPS. LiDAR uses laser measurements to map the shape and elevation of terrain. RTK GPS can provide highly precise positioning, helping place captured images and measurements more accurately. Put simply, the camera shows what is there, while mapping and positioning technologies help establish where exactly it is and, in some cases, how high or low the land lies. That information can be particularly useful in flood-prone areas, where understanding terrain, drainage channels, embankments and floodplains can help authorities prepare for and respond to flooding. Before a flood: building a clearer picture Drones do not have to wait for a disaster to strike. By stitching together hundreds of aerial photographs, drones can turn a flooded landscape into detailed maps that show rescuers what has changed and where. Photograph: (Instagram/ @garudaaerospace ) Before the monsoon, aerial surveys can document rivers, drainage channels, embankments, bridges and other infrastructure. Detailed terrain maps can help identify low-lying areas and provide a better understanding of how water could move across a landscape. The real value is having a before picture. Once a flood occurs, that earlier map can be compared with fresh drone imagery to understand what has changed. During a flood: helping teams find people and plan rescues This is when the technology can become particularly useful. Drones can survey large or dangerous areas, identify flooded roads and damaged infrastructure, and give emergency teams additional information when deciding where to send rescue personnel and supplies. Depending on the equipment being used, thermal cameras can also help detect heat signatures during search-and-rescue operations. Payload-carrying drones can deliver essentials such as food, water or medical supplies to locations that rescuers cannot immediately reach. Importantly, drones are not a replacement for boats, rescue workers or helicopters. Their role is to provide another layer of information, helping those teams understand the situation before and during an operation. After the water recedes: the map still matters A drone's job does not necessarily end when the floodwater goes down. Fresh aerial imagery can help document damage to roads, bridges, buildings, embankments and agricultural land. Engineers and authorities can use this information to assess damage, plan repairs and identify areas that may need stronger protection before the next flood. Even after the waters recede, aerial imagery can help document damaged infrastructure and guide recovery, repairs and future flood preparedness. Photograph: ( LinkedIn/@OEA Consults LTD ) Over time, these aerial records can also provide a visual history of how a particular area has changed and responded to flooding. That is perhaps the most useful way to look at drones in disaster response. A flood can change a landscape within hours. For rescuers on the ground, understanding those changes quickly can make a difficult situation easier to navigate. By giving emergency teams a clearer view of what is happening below, drones can help turn aerial data into better-informed, faster action when it matters most. Sources: 'Flood mapping Drone Guide' by Association for Drones, Published on 16 July 2026 'The Role of Drones in Disaster Management' by Garud Survey 'How Drones Are Used in Flood Monitoring' by Drones Now, Published on 21 march 2026.

items.title: After His Family Ran Out of Water, He Tested 600 Formulas to Build a Waterless Car Wash
items.blurb: A car wash may leave a vehicle sparkling clean, but it can also leave behind something far more precious — litres of water wasted in the process. With a traditional car wash using around 25 litres of water for a single vehicle, the everyday act of keeping our cars clean can quietly add to the pressure on an already stretched resource. And in a country where many cities face water shortages every summer, one Pune entrepreneur began wondering: what if we could wash cars without water at all? That question led Nitin, the founder of Go Waterless, on a two-year journey to find an unlikely alternative. It started with a water shortage While working at his family’s automobile business, Nitin had seen the same problem return every summer. The borewells would dry up, leaving little or no water to wash customers’ cars. For Nitin, it was more than an inconvenience. If there was no water, there was no way to continue the car-washing business. After testing nearly 600 formulations, Nitin developed a plant-based cleaner that uses just 100 ml of solution instead of roughly 25 litres of water for a conventional car wash. So, instead of looking for another source of water, he decided to eliminate the need for it all together. 600 formulas later The idea was easier imagined than executed. Nitin spent two years experimenting with different formulations, trying nearly 600 formulas before arriving at a plant-based cleaner that could safely clean cars without water. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) The journey also came with its share of doubts. His wife mortgaged her jewellery to support the venture, while members of his family wondered if Nitin had taken things too far. But he kept going. Eventually, he developed a cleaner made using a unique blend of five plant extracts. The formulation is anti-corrosive, disinfecting and designed to leave cars streak-free. Most importantly, just 100 ml of the solution can replace the roughly 25 litres of water used in a conventional car wash. From a bold experiment to 214 franchises What began as Nitin’s attempt to solve a water shortage at his family business has since grown into Go Waterless, which now has 214 franchises across 22 states, with international orders coming in too. From a summer water shortage to a growing business, Nitin’s idea is helping save water one car at a time. From an initial investment of around Rs 10 lakh, the business has grown to around Rs 10 crore in five years. Yet, beyond the numbers, Nitin’s larger goal remains to reduce water wastage, one car at a time. Because sometimes, saving a precious resource doesn’t require changing the way we live — it simply means doing everyday things a little differently.

items.title: This Forester Spotted a Strange Crab on Patrol. It Led to the Discovery of a New Species in Karnataka
items.blurb: On a routine forest patrol in Karnataka’s Mookambika Wildlife Sanctuary, beat forester Ajmeer K noticed something that many people might have walked past. “A freshwater crab moved across the forest floor, but its colour and unusual movement caught his attention. He, who regularly patrols the forests of the Kollur range, decided to look closer. That small moment of inquisitiveness has now led to the scientific discovery of a new species,” as reported by The Times of India . The crab has been named Ghatiana karnataka, and its discovery adds another chapter to what scientists already know about the extraordinary biodiversity of the Western Ghats. Ajmeer co-authored the scientific description with Santanu Mitra of the Zoological Survey of India. Their research was recently published in the journal Species. It began with a closer look Ajmeer first noticed the crab during a patrol in the Kollur range last year. Its unusual colour and the way it moved made him curious enough to investigate instead of simply continuing on his route. He contacted Santanu, who also suspected that the crab might represent an undocumented species . Following the necessary permissions from the forest department, specimens were collected for a detailed taxonomic study. Researchers examined both male and female crabs, documenting their physical characteristics, colouration and habitat before confirming the species as new to science. The crab has been named Ghatiana karnataka, and its discovery adds another chapter. Photograph: (Deccan Herald) That process matters because spotting an unfamiliar animal is only the beginning. To establish a new species scientifically, researchers have to show that it is distinct from species already known. Meet Ghatiana karnataka The newly described crab belongs to the genus Ghatiana, a group of freshwater crabs found only in the Western Ghats. The male has a predominantly dark-purple body with a striking light-pink to mauve V-shaped marking on the front of its shell, known as the carapace. Females look different, with a grey-violet front and dark grey-brown rear. The species is currently confirmed from Mavinakaru, near Kollur, although Ajmeer’s observations suggest that similar crabs occur across a much wider stretch of forest. Hidden among rocks and trees These crabs are not animals one is likely to notice easily. They live in highly moist evergreen and semi-evergreen forests , making use of tiny natural shelters created by the landscape. They have been found in crevices between boulders, water-filled holes in laterite rocks, and damp cavities in trees. The surrounding landscape is kept humid by perennial rivers including the Souparnika, Mavinakaru, and Jadkal. During the monsoon, the crabs may venture across wet laterite rocks. When the forest becomes drier, they retreat into moist tree hollows and rock cavities. Their diet is just as closely tied to the forest. Decaying plant matter, bark, algae, and other organic material provide food. Not the first Ghat crab from Karnataka The discovery is significant, but it is also a reminder of how much remains to be documented in the Western Ghats. The genus Ghatiana now has 15 known species, all endemic to the Western Ghats. “With Ghatiana karnataka, Karnataka has eight recorded species in the genus,” according to The Times of India . Ajmeer first noticed the crab during a patrol in the Kollur range last year. Photograph: (Wikipedia (representational image)) This is not the first time an unexpected freshwater crab has appeared from Karnataka’s forests. Earlier discoveries have included other Ghatiana species, some found by forest staff and naturalists who noticed unusual crabs during their time in the field. A name for a state’s biodiversity Ajmeer initially hoped the crab might be named after the area where it was found. Instead, Mitra suggested Karnataka as its species name, recognising the state’s extraordinary biodiversity . For Ajmeer, the discovery also reflects something more personal. Originally from Hosapete in Vijayanagara district, he holds a BA degree and has developed a strong interest in documenting the wildlife he encounters during his forest duties. His role may be described as that of a beat forester, but his daily work puts him in places that scientists cannot always reach regularly. Every patrol can bring him face to face with something unusual. There is still so much to find The observation of Ghatiana, Karnataka, is more than the addition of another name to a scientific list. It shows how much the Western Ghats can still reveal when people pay attention to the small details around them. A crab hiding inside a damp tree cavity may seem insignificant against the vastness of a rainforest. But it can represent a species that science had not formally recognised before. Researchers examined both male and female crabs, documenting their physical characteristics, colouration and habitat before confirming the species. Photograph: (Deccan Herald) Kundapur Deputy Conservator of Forests Ruthren P said the discovery highlights how much of the region’s biodiversity remains undocumented. He also stressed that forest staff who take an interest in research and biodiversity should be encouraged and supported, as reported by The Times of India . For Ajmeer, it began with something wonderfully simple. He noticed a crab that looked different. And instead of walking past it, he stopped to find out why.

items.title: Coimbatore Designer Uses Maps & Fruit Models To Teach 354 Blind Students
items.blurb: In a government classroom in Tamil Nadu, a young girl sits at her desk, her head bent in concentration. Her fingers move slowly across a raised map placed in front of her, tracing its curved lines, edges and borders. She has heard teachers describe Tamil Nadu before. Now, its shape is taking form beneath her fingertips. She can follow the outline of the state and trace the curve of its coastline with her own hands. For visually impaired children like her, a moment like this can mark the difference between memorising a description and understanding what it means. A map becomes something they can explore. A fruit has a shape they can recognise. A science diagram becomes something their fingers can follow and remember. Across Tamil Nadu, tactile learning materials are bringing this experience into government schools for visually impaired students. Raised maps, models of fruits, science diagrams and tactile Braille books are helping children understand concepts that have long depended heavily on verbal descriptions, repetition and memory. This raised map of India is designed for visually impaired students to explore by touch.] Behind these materials is Tactile Braille India, a Coimbatore-based venture founded by Prabhu. It has entered into an MoU with the Tamil Nadu government to provide tactile learning materials to government schools for visually impaired students. So far, the materials have reached 10 government schools across 10 districts in Tamil Nadu, benefiting around 354 students. The work began with a question that stayed with Prabhu: How could concepts designed to be understood visually be made accessible through touch? The question that made Prabhu look beyond words Prabhu came to this work from a background far removed from education. Born into a farming family, he grew up around the land, hard work and limited resources. After completing his BCom degree, he began working with digital and visual content. His work included 2D and 3D graphics, HTML, website design and the development of e-learning platforms. Prabhu holds a raised map of India alongside students at a Tactile Braille India display. That experience taught him to think about how information could be communicated visually and digitally. It would later become relevant to a very different challenge: translating visual concepts into forms that visually impaired students could understand through touch. It was during this phase of his life that he first encountered Braille and began thinking about its possibilities and limitations. “I realised that visually impaired students were learning only words and numbers,” Prabhu recalls. “They could read text, but they had no way to understand shapes, maps or diagrams. Geography, science, even simple objects, everything was abstract.” The realisation stayed with him. If sighted children could look at a map, diagram or shape and build an understanding of it, Prabhu wondered how the same concepts could be made accessible to children who learnt through touch. In 2011, he began studying tactile education systems used in India and Europe. He learnt how raised lines could represent visual information, how textures could explain geography and biology, and how everyday objects could be translated into tactile form. A tactile learning book combines Braille, numbers, alphabets and familiar shapes. In 2017, he began working with Braille-based learning materials using conventional Braille methods. Then, in 2023, he expanded this work into tactile learning and started the venture under the name Tactile Braille India. His focus grew to include tactile maps, diagrams, models and other learning materials that allow visually impaired students to understand concepts through touch. Over the years, Prabhu imported specialised machines, experimented with materials and worked on tactile Braille books, raised maps, fruit models and science diagrams. “Braille teaches words. But tactile graphics teach the world,” he says. The cost of putting a map beneath a child’s fingers Creating these materials brought another challenge: cost. Prabhu says even a blank Braille book can cost around Rs 3,000, while the machines used for tactile printing are expensive imports. For schools with limited resources, that can make specialised learning material difficult to access. “I didn’t want cost to become another barrier,” Prabhu explains. “If these materials were too expensive, schools would never be able to use them.” Tactile Braille India’s learning book uses raised lines and Braille to explain space. He began importing specialised paper himself, handling printing in-house and absorbing much of the production expense. Today, through Tactile Braille India, he supplies tactile Braille books containing maps and science diagrams, along with learning models, to the Tamil Nadu government at a reduced cost. “My time, my effort, everything I do is so that blind children can learn independently, without depending on anyone,” he says. “For me, this was never about business. If blind children can learn on their own, that itself is happiness.” Prabhu also points to a larger gap that drives his work. “Only about 25–30 percent of visually impaired students in India receive meaningful access to education,” he says. “I want that number to grow.” A tactile learning page uses raised outlines to explain parts of plants and their growth. The work has travelled beyond Tamil Nadu too. Prabhu has supplied tactile model books and learning materials through organisations working with visually impaired students in around 11 other states, including Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Maharashtra. Through these networks, the materials have reached approximately 1,250 students outside Tamil Nadu. In his home state, the MoU with the Tamil Nadu government has brought the materials into government schools for visually impaired students. According to Prabhu, tactile learning tools are also being integrated into the official syllabus, giving students another way to engage with subjects that rely heavily on visual concepts. A tactile learning page uses raised outlines and Braille to explain the human body. “When I think about how my work is helping blind children understand the world,” he says, “it gives me real happiness.” What changed inside a Pudukkottai classroom The difference becomes easier to understand inside the Government Middle School for the Visually Impaired in Pudukkottai district. Here, headmaster Vadivelan has watched students encounter concepts through tactile books and models. “Earlier, our students learnt only alphabets, numbers and basic words,” he says. “They had no idea what a fruit looked like, what the map of India felt like, or what a kidney or heart was. These were things they simply could not imagine.” A tactile science page explains the human kidney using raised outlines and Braille labels. Science and geography were particularly difficult. Teachers relied heavily on verbal explanations, describing shapes, borders, organs and other concepts while students tried to build a mental picture of something they could not physically explore. Tactile materials have given them another way in. “For the first time, students can explore concepts on their own. They can feel shapes, follow outlines and understand spatial relationships. The government supporting this initiative through the syllabus has given our children an opportunity they never had before,” Vadivelan says. A student explores a tactile learning book with raised drawings, Braille and labels. Teachers say the students are more engaged, ask more questions and retain concepts better. Lessons that once felt distant are becoming easier to explore and revisit. For two students in the school, that change can be understood through something as simple as a map and an apple. The day Vignesh could feel Tamil Nadu’s coastline For Vignesh, a Class 8 student, geography was once one of the most confusing subjects in school. His teachers spoke about borders, coastlines and neighbouring states. He could listen to the descriptions and remember the words, but the shapes behind those words remained abstract. That changed the day a tactile map was placed on his desk. Vignesh ran his fingers over its raised surface, paused and retraced the lines. His teacher told him, “This is Tamil Nadu.” For the first time, he could feel the outline of his own state. His fingertips followed the curve of the coastline and the edges where one region met another. “Earlier, I could only imagine what the teacher described. Now I can understand it myself. When I touched the map, I felt where Tamil Nadu begins and ends. It stayed in my mind,” says Vignesh. Vignesh reads a Braille book at the Government Middle School for the Visually Impaired. His teachers noticed a change after that lesson. Vignesh began asking more questions in class. During free periods, he returned to the tactile map, tracing it again and again and growing more confident with every pass of his fingers. Geography, once a subject he feared, had become something he could grasp, quite literally. When Harini recognised an apple without guessing For Harini, a Class 7 student, the challenge lay closer to everyday life. She had heard descriptions of fruits all her life: round, smooth, long and soft. She knew their names, but those words had not given her a clear understanding of their shapes. “I knew the names,” she says, “but I didn’t know their shape.” Then tactile diagrams of fruits were introduced in her classroom. Using her fingertips, Harini traced the raised outline of a mango and then an apple. She followed their curves and edges, feeling the differences between their shapes. Harini uses a tactile Braille book designed to help students understand shapes through touch. Later, her teacher placed a real apple in her hand. The shape felt familiar. It matched what her fingers had already explored on the page. “It felt exactly like what I studied,” she says, her voice bright. “I was not guessing anymore. I knew.” That moment gave her greater confidence in class and in her own understanding. Her teachers say Harini now participates more actively, particularly during lessons involving objects and diagrams. “For the first time,” she says, “I feel like I understand the world a little better.” ‘They feel capable’ For visually impaired students, tactile learning creates space for a different kind of classroom experience. Students can return to a map, retrace a diagram or explore a model at their own pace. They can build an understanding of a shape through their own hands and revisit it whenever they need to. Harini traces a raised diagram in a tactile Braille book during a classroom learning session. That independence matters to the educators working with them. “When children realise they can understand things on their own, it changes how they see themselves,” a teacher notes. “They feel capable.” For Prabhu, that growing confidence is also what gives years of experimentation, designing and production their meaning. “When I see children confidently tracing maps or explaining shapes, I feel my work has meaning,” he says. “They are no longer limited by what they cannot see. All my effort is for the independence of visually impaired students.” For Vignesh, a coastline now has a curve he can follow. For Harini, the shape of an apple is something she can recognise instead of guessing. Across the classrooms these materials have reached, raised lines, maps, diagrams and models are giving students another way to encounter the world around them, one they can explore with their own hands and understand for themselves.
